extracted.intended_audience: patent attorneys, administrative law scholars, judges, policymakers, and informed practitioners concerned with USPTO rulemaking and § 101 guidance
extracted.subtask_description: Analyze whether USPTO documents (guidance, examples, memos) constitute substantive (legislative) rules requiring APA notice-and-comment and what level of judicial deference they merit under Chevron or Skidmore. Applies to assessing §101 subject-matter-eligibility materials and similar agency guidance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Chevron deference applies only to substantive rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Only rules receive Chevron deference; when the PTO speaks under a rule, its decisions and interpretations are accorded substantial weight by reviewing courts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because Chevron applies to legislative/substantive rules, the classification of a PTO statement as a binding rule versus guidance determines whether courts must defer under Chevron. If the PTO lacks substantive rulemaking power, Chevron does not apply (e.g., Fed. Cir. holding that 'the rule of controlling deference set forth in Chevron does not apply').

rubrics_metrics.name: Guidance is entitled only to persuasive (Skidmore) weight
rubrics_metrics.description: When the Patent Office issues guidance rather than substantive rules, courts consider those documents only to the extent they are persuasive (Skidmore), not controlling.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Skidmore deference depends on the persuasiveness of the agency's reasoning and consistency. Courts vary: some district courts call USPTO guidance 'persuasive' or use it 'as a resource,' while certain Federal Circuit panels have explicitly declined even Skidmore deference for narrow guidance items (e.g., hypothetical examples).

rubrics_metrics.name: Statutory grant of substantive rulemaking authority
rubrics_metrics.description: An agency must have a specific grant of substantive rulemaking authority from Congress to promulgate legislative (substantive) rules.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Absent a specific statutory grant, the Patent Office may promulgate rules governing its internal procedures and nonbinding interpretive or guidance documents but cannot validly promulgate substantive rules setting patentability law. Courts look for an express delegation of legislative-rule power.

rubrics_metrics.name: APA §553 procedural requirements control substantive rulemaking
rubrics_metrics.description: The APA §553 sets procedures (notice-and-comment) agencies must follow for rulemaking, and interpretive rules/statements of policy are generally exempt.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a PTO statement qualifies as a substantive (legislative) rule, it must comply with §553's notice-and-comment procedures unless a narrow statutory exception applies. Failure to follow §553 can invalidate substantive rules; agencies sometimes claim 'good cause' to avoid notice-and-comment when impracticable or contrary to public interest.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpretive-rule critical feature: advising the public of agency’s construction
rubrics_metrics.description: Interpretive rules are issued to advise the public of the agency’s construction of the statutes and rules it administers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts (and the Supreme Court in Perez) treat this advisory function as a hallmark of interpretive rules, but the precise boundary between interpretive and legislative rules remains contested and 'not further defined by the APA.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Whether the statement changes law or tracks precedent
rubrics_metrics.description: A key clue: does the agency statement restate and track prior judicial/board precedent, or does it effect a change in the law?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If language 'largely tracks' prior decisional history (as in ALDF's framing of the 1987 notice), courts are likely to view it as interpretive. Language that goes beyond restating precedent (e.g., adding new categorical exclusions) may exceed authority and suggest substantive rulemaking.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adverse effect on individual rights/obligations test
rubrics_metrics.description: Limiting agency or examiner discretion renders a rule substantive only when that limitation has an adverse effect on an individual’s rights or obligations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: ALDF emphasizes that a mere restriction of examiner discretion does not equal a substantive rule unless applicants or affected parties are adversely affected. Expansion of eligibility (making rejections less likely) typically does not constitute adverse effect under this test.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expansion vs restriction of eligibility matters for 'adverse effect' analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether a PTO notice expands or restricts §101 eligibility affects whether parties are 'adversely affected' and thus whether the notice is substantive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If mandatory, a notice that causes examiners to refrain from issuing §101 rejections (i.e., expands eligibility) does not adversely affect applicants and thus is less likely to be deemed substantive. Conversely, notices that restrict eligibility may adversely affect rights and lean toward substantive classification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Whether guidance is genuinely interpretative of a statute or effectively creating common law
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess whether the PTO is interpreting an enabling statute/regulation or is effectively making law (e.g., interpreting judicially created doctrines like 'abstract idea' or 'law of nature').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because §101’s modern doctrine derives largely from judicial common law, PTO guidance that purports to 'interpret' concepts not evident on the statute’s face may be functionally legislative. Courts examine whether the guidance is faithful to the statute and controlling precedent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consistency/conflict with Federal Circuit precedent
rubrics_metrics.description: Guidance that conflicts with earlier or controlling Federal Circuit holdings may not be a faithful interpretation and weakens claims of interpretive status.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Panel decisions control unless overruled en banc; guidance adopting later, conflicting panel holdings may not reflect correct law. Courts will compare guidance to the landscape of Federal Circuit authority when classifying it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Whether guidance will be subject to testing through enforcement or appeals
rubrics_metrics.description: Rules that set enforcement criteria or deregulatory policies lose the 'tested-by-enforcement' safeguard and are more problematic when issued as guidance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Scholars note that interpretive rules that set minimum criteria or reduce rejections are unlikely to be tested by enforcement actions, meaning potential errors in guidance may persist without judicial correction. The absence of a challenged rejection (or lack of appeals) weakens the agency’s accountability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Form and content clues: hypotheticals and examples vs general statements
rubrics_metrics.description: The format of a guidance item (e.g., a hypothetical example vs a general interpretive memorandum) affects how persuasive or binding courts regard it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts have been willing to treat hypotheticals and single examples (e.g., 'Example 29') as nonbinding and have declined deference to narrow illustrative statements; more comprehensive, central statements in guidance may attract greater persuasive force but still fall short of Chevron unless rulemaking procedures were used.

rubrics_metrics.name: PTAB treatment can amplify guidance’s practical authority
rubrics_metrics.description: The Patent Trial and Appeal Board’s internal adherence to PTO guidance (including citing and applying it in decisions) can make guidance effectively authoritative within agency adjudication.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: PTAB opinions have cited and applied PTO guidance to sustain examiner rejections, and a precedential PTAB opinion embracing guidance might increase the document’s practical weight and may be argued to deserve deference by reviewing courts, potentially creating a 'backdoor' path to deference.

rubrics_metrics.name: Agency’s ability to invoke 'good cause' to avoid notice-and-comment
rubrics_metrics.description: Even when APA §553 would ordinarily require notice-and-comment, an agency may claim 'good cause' to bypass that procedure if compliance is impracticable, unnecessary, or contrary to the public interest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a statutory allowance that can justify issuing interpretive or procedural changes without notice, but courts scrutinize 'good cause' claims; its availability complicates classification and procedural compliance analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: High stakes and systemic costs in patent context
rubrics_metrics.description: The particular stakes of patent eligibility (broad rights, follow-on innovation costs, consumer impacts) complicate reliance on guidance rather than formal rulemaking.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because PTO guidance on §101 can expand or contract the scope of government-sponsored monopolies, its issuance without notice-and-comment can shift significant rights and impose 'dynamic costs' on downstream innovators and the public. Courts and scholars treat these practical consequences as relevant to whether formal procedures should have been required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Close textual correspondence with board or judicial language supports interpretive classification
rubrics_metrics.description: When guidance language largely mirrors prior Board or judicial language, courts are likely to view it as interpretive rather than substantive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In ALDF the court emphasized that the 1987 notice 'largely tracks the above history and the language of Allen,' supporting the conclusion that it represented an interpretation of precedent rather than a change in law; deviating textual elements (e.g., novel categorical exclusions) raise red flags.
